title: A Tax Collector, a King, a City
overview: As Jesus nears Jerusalem, he welcomes a despised tax collector, tells a story about a king who goes away, enters the city to cheers, weeps over its coming fall, and clears traders out of the temple.

parts.label: Zacchaeus up a tree (vv. 1-10)
parts.note: Tax collectors gathered money for the Roman system and were widely seen as cheats, so the crowd is shocked when Jesus chooses to stay with a rich chief collector. Zacchaeus gives half his wealth to the poor and promises fourfold repayment to anyone he cheated, well beyond the law's usual demand of the amount plus a fifth, and Jesus says he too belongs among Abraham's people.

parts.label: Why this story now (vv. 11-14)
parts.note: People expected God's kingdom to appear the moment Jesus reached Jerusalem, so he tells of a nobleman who must first travel far away to be made king. Many scholars think this echoes Archelaus, a son of Herod, who went to Rome to be confirmed as ruler while some of his subjects sent a delegation to oppose him.

parts.label: Servants and their money (vv. 15-27)
parts.note: Each servant gets one mina, about a hundred days' wages; those who put it to work are rewarded, while the one who hid it out of fear loses it, which Christians usually read as being faithful with what God entrusts until Jesus returns. The story ends brutally with the king ordering his opponents killed, and readers differ on whether this king pictures Jesus or stands in contrast to him.

parts.label: Riding into Jerusalem (vv. 28-40)
parts.note: Jesus rides in on a young colt no one has ridden, people spread their cloaks on the road as a way of honoring a king, and his followers cheer with words drawn from Psalm 118. When some Pharisees, members of a strict religious group, tell him to quiet them, he says the stones themselves would shout.

parts.label: Tears over the city (vv. 41-44)
parts.note: Jesus weeps as he foresees Jerusalem surrounded, besieged and flattened because it did not recognize the time when God came to it. Roman armies did besiege and destroy the city in the year 70.

parts.label: Clearing the temple (vv. 45-48)
parts.note: Jesus drives out those selling in the temple courts, quoting Isaiah's call for a house of prayer and Jeremiah's charge that it had become a hideout for robbers. The religious leaders were looking for a way to kill him, but they could not act because ordinary people hung on his every word.

disagreement: Christians differ over whether the harsh king in the parable of the minas stands for Jesus and his coming judgment, as traditionally read, or is a picture of worldly power set against the kind of king Jesus is.
think: What do you think changes a person more deeply: being confronted with their wrongs, or being unexpectedly welcomed?
